cues.text: Meet T-MINUS. Build a CubeSat and its rocket, launch it with real physics, and learn from every failure.
Choose a mission. FloodWatch-1: photograph the Indus floods for thirty days, within a strict budget, mass, power and data limit.
In the Integration Bay we install every subsystem. Live budgets show mass, cost, power, battery and data, each with a one-line why.
Then we wire it. Every cable follows real engineering rules, and appears on the satellite in three D.
Now the rocket. Parts stack bottom-first, and mistakes are refused with a reason. Every joint is bolted in star order, in three torque passes.
But here we rush joint one: clockwise, one pass, three bolts missing. HOUSTON, the built-in mentor, scans the build and flags it.
At the pad the checklist shows the failing joint, and the crew launches anyway.
Real physics takes over: gravity, drag, and thrust that changes with altitude.
The debrief doesn't just say you failed. It traces the cause: joint one, rushed bolting, three missing bolts.
So we fix it: all twelve bolts, in star order, three passes. Then we launch again.
Orbit achieved, and the CubeSat deploys.
Thirty simulated days of operations. Ninety-seven out of a hundred, three stars, and real NASA Landsat flood images, at our camera's resolution.
There is more: a detailed Saturn V Moonshot mission, a Failure Lab with Apollo twelve, a searchable Space Guide, and it works on phones and tablets.
T-MINUS. Build it. Launch it. Learn from it.
